utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. I was informed, Mr. Karadzic, that you have something to raise in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. We were thinking it would be better to do this without the witness so that what I'm going to present to the Trial Chamber in no way affects his evidence. Why did we ask for 40 hours? In other words, why do we believe that this is one of the key witnesses? If we miss this opportunity to confront the witness and the opportunity for all of us in this courtroom to learn something about the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we may perhaps never have another witness who will be able to present this to us from such close quarters. This man was in charge of crime prevention, prosecution, and bringing to justice all criminals in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was right at the source. He was able to know about everything that was going on in the country, and he knew it. That's how things worked in Republika Srpska, where he was also a justice minister. And the last stage, the prosecution of crimes, was in his jurisdiction, as was the establishment of the judicial system and so on. I would recommend to your attention from the pre-trial brief, paragraphs from 109 to 117 inclusive, referring only to what the Prosecution believes to be the gist of the joint criminal enterprise as regarding the MUP, and only regarding the MUP. In these eight or nine paragraphs, it says: [In English] "The MUP played a significant role in establishing and maintaining Bosnian Serb authority over the territory and implementing the common criminal purpose." [Interpretation] And so on. In 110: [In English] "Prior to its division, Karadzic contemplated the division of the MUP as an essential complement of the division of B and H and the realisation of the final goal to break off with Muslims and Croats forever." [Interpretation] 111, the last one, paragraph 2: [In English] "The minister of justice was responsible for implementing the decision, and he took immediate steps toward its implementation." [Interpretation] 112 is also important and implies that we are in some sort of joint enterprise. 113 says: [In English] "When a high level Serb member of the BH MUP resisted the division of the MUP, he was summoned to a meeting with Karadzic, Krajisnik, Stanisic, Mandic, and others, and attacked for failing to support the division of the MUP. He tendered his resignation." [Interpretation] 114: [In English] "Stanisic and Mandic who reported directly to Karadzic and Krajisnik, as explained above, played a critical role in the organised detention and expulsion of Muslims and Croats," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] This is only regarding the MUP. Regarding paramilitary and volunteer units, between which the Prosecution puts a sign of equality, which is far from the truth, far from reality. There are also allegations in paragraphs 3 to 6 and another paragraph in the pre-trial brief, and in Count 3, sniping isn't Sarajevo, one count involving Srebrenica, and so on. Who will present to us the essence which the Defence claims is diametrically opposite to what is written in the indictment and that some Prosecution experts and witnesses present here, and even mislead the Prosecution into believing things to be completely different than they were? This witness was a participant and witness to everything that happened from the first multi-party elections to the end of 1992. You were able to see how I speak to several major protagonists within one day, trying to preserve the peace. The Prosecution is trying to say I'm setting the stage for war, but, in fact, I'm trying to preserve peace. That's what you can see in these intercepts. Throughout 1991 and 1992, which this witness can speak about, there were so many critical events in one day that I really have to ask for your patience to put this jigsaw puzzle together, because if we miss a piece, you won't be able to understand the whole picture. And that is the gist of this process, as a whole. That's why I believe that, for instance, this first part about the division of the MUP is crucial. It goes in parallel with the peace conference. We are doing our best to avoid any deterioration -- any further deterioration of the political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, while facing a conspiracy involving all the state organs in which Muslims and Croats, but primarily Muslims, hold two-thirds of the power. All this is about the pre-war period, and we are getting close to April and the outbreak of the war, and we will then be able to present to the Trial Chamber every last detail of what was going on, what was inevitable, what our choices were, what we could have done, and what we actually did. That is why I believe this is probably the key witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I do not disagree at all that this witness is a very important witness. The point I raised yesterday was that whether you could have been more efficient in putting questions, whether you should have -- whether you had to spend all six hours in order to deal with those personnel issues. We are not trying to -- we are not trying to publish a white book on the history of the BiH. This is a criminal trial which deals with the charges against you. Please bear that in mind, and then be as efficient as possible, and please concentrate on the events which covers the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And I would add, Dr. Karadzic, that we will take what you've just said into account when considering the submission that you make which I anticipate is, although you didn't say so, what, in effect, you're asking for is an extension of the 20 hours suggested. As we've said all along, those figures are not set in stone. They are dependent upon what happens on a day-to-day basis. And if the Trial Chamber is of the view that your submission has merit, then it will be reflected in any decision that's made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I wonder about one other thing. Since this witness has been accepted as a Court witness, could the Defence possibly offer another set of exhibits so that the witness can only identify them, without going through each and every one of them in detail, as they reflect some typical phenomena?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you put them in writing in the very immediate future so that we can hear from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should include the portions you want to tender amongst the transcript of his evidence in Stanisic and Zupljanin. Thank you. And if I can take this opportunity to hear from Mr. Tieger that we couldn't deal with, we were short of time two days ago, about your suggestion to tender all the Assembly minutes. I asked you where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we're prepared simply to engage in the logistics of marking and admitting those. We have submitted to the Defence, to the Registry, and to the Court Officers the list of Assembly sessions that were referenced in the Donia reports. I anticipated that once we found the first opportunity to do that, the Registrar could just go down the list and, as we have done for, for example, associated exhibits, just give them numbers and they are admitted. So it was my understanding that only -- that barring any issue with the Court, only the technical logistics of giving the Assembly sessions numbers and having them formally admitted remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, we are going with them all, aren't we? You're not going to use them, all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, I'm sure that in -- well, a couple of issues surrounding those. First of all, the Court will recall Mr. Robinson's suggestion earlier that among the official documents that should be admitted in their entirety, we could begin with the Assembly sessions. That was a suggestion with which the Prosecution agreed. In this particular case, the issue arose about the contextualisation of the references in the Donia report. The Prosecution indicated that it anticipated that that problem would be resolved by the admission of the Assembly sessions referenced in the reports, in their entirety. Mr. Robinson was in agreement. I understand Dr. Karadzic is as well. So the Court may well be right that -- well, the Court is, I think, correct that over time, one way or another, all the Assembly sessions will be admitted. But this seemed to be an appropriate moment for the admission of those Assembly sessions referenced in the Donia report, for the reasons I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to be clear, that your intention is to tender those Assembly session minutes or transcripts that haven't been tendered yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, and there are -- among the Assembly sessions that were referenced in Dr. Donia's reports are Assembly sessions that have already been admitted. Those were indicated expressly in the chart provided by the Prosecution, so we indicated the sessions, referenced in their entirety, and then also highlighted specifically those which had already been admitted so there wouldn't be confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The whole point behind this is just convenience, in terms of conduct of trial, without going into the practice of tendering them, admitting them separately --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in light of the fact that they are going to be used in the future in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And with respect to that over-arching principle, we could move forward to admit all of the Assembly sessions, which was essentially a joint request by the Prosecution and Defence. In this particular instance, it just encompasses those Assembly sessions specifically referenced in the Donia reports, so it's a sub-set of the entirety of the Assembly sessions. But I take the Court's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any observation on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you have said, Your Excellency, I believe that at the end of the day, everything will be admitted in one way or another. I do not overestimate the words of the MPs, because the main enactments are the Constitution, the laws, et cetera, but I don't mind them being admitted. Part of this material is complementary between the Prosecution and the Defence, and some of it is in favour of one side or another. So what they do not tender, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will come back to that issue later on. Yes, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one small scheduling issue I wanted to raise with the Court. It would be extremely helpful for the Prosecution, in terms of scheduling, if the Court could provide an indication of the time it will allot for the cross-examination of Mr. Mandilovic. I mention that for obvious reasons, the normal scheduling issues, but also because in light of the convergence of the upcoming summer recess and the fact that one of the remaining witnesses before then is locked into particular dates, there is a serious risk that one of the witnesses will have to actually travel back and forth three times for this same appearance. I'm confident that's something the Court wants to avoid, even if it means the possibility that we'll have some hours that are left open because there's an unexpected opening in the schedule. We simply don't want to oblige the witness to do that, and I'm sure the Court shares that concern. But it would help us to know the likelihood of that risk if the Court could advise us of how much time it will allot for the cross-examination of Mr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is Mr. Mandilovic the one who we'll hear after Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And have we received the estimate from the Defence yet? I don't remember we received their estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe we've had the time. Just a moment. I don't think -- I'm not sure we sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm virtually certain that's the case, and I think the request was for 14 hours. But I'll double-check on that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll double-check as well. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 14 hours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We had certain matters to deal with in the absence of yourself, so we'll begin today. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Minister.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are drawing close to the key events in April, and we have to build up the story brick by brick. Can I call up in e-court 65 ter 6585, unless it already has a P number. 6585. While we're waiting, Mr. Mandic, let me refresh your memory. If you'll recall, towards the end of 1991 and early 1992, Ambassador Wijnaendts and later Lord Carrington and Cutileiro came to our country, and the peace conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina began within the framework of the broader Conference on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you remember, on the 23rd of February, we reached the first agreement ever, at least the outlines of an agreement that was supposed to be further developed, and that is this Statement of Principles. We've got it on the screen now. This is the foundation of the solution to the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina to this day. We need English page 5 -- English page 2 and Serbian 3. In fact, the Serbian starting with the bottom of page 2 and then going on to page 3. Serbian 3, English 2. This passage is the about the jurisdiction of the constituent units of the complex Bosnian state, and in paragraph 2, may I draw your attention to this passage that concerns the Assembly and the government, and all the provisions about the jurisdictions of the constituent units.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Everyone can read for themselves. But towards the bottom of this paragraph, we see an enumeration "culture," but towards the bottom, "forestry, social welfare, police security," et cetera. Has it remained in effect to this day that constituent units will govern police affairs independently, but supervised by a unified policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was so stipulated in the Dayton Accords and now in the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that constituent units have their own governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that various possibilities for these divisions of competencies were discussed during the peace conferences, but it was never in question that the police would be within the jurisdiction of the entities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that I am being too fast. I have to be more careful. So this is the first brick in that edifice that was adopted and later only further developed. Do you remember it was the position of the Serbian, the Croat, but also the Muslim side was that things that have once been agreed upon not be discussed anymore, but, rather, that we should move on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was reported by the media, and that's the information we got in the Ministry of the Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was only in 1993, since there were certain inconsistencies in comparison with what had been agreed already, the principle was introduced in 1993 by Stoltenberg that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I wasn't in Bosnia then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been admitted as Exhibit P798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I raise one minor matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the accused could advise us if he's using a document that's not on the list of the 1200 documents he notified us that he would be using. I understand that happens. I'm not suggesting there's any prejudice in the use of this particular document. But it does save us the trouble of looking through the entirety of the list as soon as he announces it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karadzic, you must have heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would just like to say that this was adopted on the 23rd of February. However, it is identical to what it was that was adopted in March, as the final version. So nothing was changed in this version until the 18th of March. And this is a document that was admitted as a P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that is not the issue, Mr. Karadzic. It's your notice to the other side as to the documents which you are going to use during your cross-examination. You should advise the Prosecution as to the document if there's any changes or any additions to those documents. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If we look at things that way, perhaps it would be a good idea to admit this part under the date of the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D1210, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Minister, I would like to remind you of the fact that these are minutes from the Presidency session, a session of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on the 2nd of March, and it had to do with the killing of a member of this wedding party and the crisis that emerged. Let us just look at this first page, and then let's move on to page 3. In English, we can keep the same page. As opposed to a transcript of the entire session, this is a record, and that reflects only the essence. We are now interested only in number 2, where it says that the tragedy and general situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially Kupres, Travnik, Zivinice, is a direct reflection of the unresolved relations within the MUP. Could we have the next page in English. The Serbian and English, yes. A bit further up. The previous page in Serbian, please: "In accordance with agreements, it is requested that within 24 hours a personnel transformation be carried out of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with agreements reached by the three leading political parties right after the republican elections." Minister, does this mean the Presidency, 14 months after the coalition government was established, and 16 or 17 months after the elections, ultimately accepted the fact that the coalition agreement regarding the MUP had not been carried out and that it had to be adopted urgently now and enforced within 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was an integral part of the requests of the SDS. Also, the implication here is that the tragic situation in the republic is a consequence of the lack of order among the state organs caused by the non-implementation of agreements in structuring the MUP. Can you remind us what it was that happened in Kupres, Travnik, Zivinice, and I think in the Neretva River Valley as well at that point in time in March?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina in those areas you referred to, and it culminated in Sarajevo, there were inter-ethnic tensions, or, rather, the inter-party agreement was not observed at these particular localities regarding the appointment of MUP officials to those positions that belonged to the Serb Democratic Party according to the inter-party agreement, or, rather, the representatives of the Serb people. I think I spoke yesterday about the killing of the father of the bridegroom because he was carrying a Serb flag in Bascarsija. We, from the Crime Prevention Service that I headed, knew who the perpetrator was, Delalic, Rasim, and that he was in a house at Bistrik. However, we were not in a position to arrest him or to take any measures because the Patriotic League and the reserve police force were guarding him. The reserve police from Stari Grad Police Station, headed by Dahic, Ismet, at that point they had between 600 and 1.000 men. Of course, all of them were ethnic Muslims, and that was a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on from this decision of the Presidency: "During the day, the perpetrators of the heinous crime in front of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Bascarsija and Sarajevo be arrested during the course of the day. "Concerning the fact that the Serb people have been experiencing a lengthy informational blockade and pressure, to conduct an urgent division of the television and radio as well as to stop broadcasting Yutel until the talks about the constitutional arrangement of Bosnia-Herzegovina are over." I would just like to look at number 6 on this page. I think it has to be somewhere around there in English as well: "To immediately dissolve the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by Ejub Ganic, as an unconstitutional organ, to urgently disarm the paramilitary formations of the Green Berets that are publicly operating in Sarajevo, protecting, inter alia, criminals who are perpetrators of crimes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is not the right page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Mr. Karadzic's question. So speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters noted that they didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was whether what is written here, does that actually pertain to what the witness has said, that the perpetrator of that crime, the fact that one member of the wedding party was killed and another wounded, and were they under the -- the perpetrators under the protection of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under their protection. And, of course, those who were protecting him were from among the ranks of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The witness also said, yes, the Green Berets and the reserve police force, they were both protecting this witness. So you are speaking about this unlawfully-increased reserve force to a level of 600 to 1.000 men in Stari Grad; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That both speakers are overlapping and speaking at a pace that is too fast for court reporting and for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you note the interpreter's note in the transcript, Mr. Karadzic? Both speakers are overlapping and speaking at a pace that is too fast for court reporting and for interpretation. Please bear that in mind; Mr. Mandic as well. Put a pause before you start answering the question, after Mr. Karadzic puts a question. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise to the interpreters. However, obviously that is why parts are not recorded. I would just like to summarise the witness's answer so that he can say yes or no to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is it: This paragraph in the request that was accepted by the Presidency implies that the Green Berets should be disarmed straight away. They were operating in public in Sarajevo, and criminals are under their protection, criminals who had perpetrated crimes. And I asked whether that implies that the murder of the member of that wedding party was also being protected by the Green Berets, and your answer was that, indeed, he was under the protection of the Green Berets, but also under the protection of the reserve police force of Stari Grad that was illegally increased to a level of 600 men. Did I summarise this properly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please, in Serbian, and I believe that it would be the same in English. Not that far away in the Serbian version. Yes, that's it, thank you. I believe it's the next page in English. No, it's the same page. Right, let's keep this English page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the first highlighted sentence: "Bearing all of this in mind, the requests presented by the Crisis Staff of the Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina were accepted, and the following was agreed upon unanimously:" And so on and so forth. And then the first bold passage says that: "This does not prejudge in any way how Bosnia-Herzegovina will be organised. That is discussed under the auspices of the European Community. These talks should be urgently continued, and the results have to take into account the interests of all three peoples as well as other citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Does the Presidency unanimously accept or adopt the recommendations of the SDS, and is it not stated that the ultimate solution would be found at the conference?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the last highlighted sentence: "To carry out as briefly as possible an agreement on the reorganisation of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina and resolve personnel matters." In English, it may be the last sentence. Can we scroll up? Oh, yes, right, that's it, yes: "To implement an agreement ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that pertain to the resolution of these personnel problems that had accumulated, and the fact that they were not being resolved actually led to the culmination of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And: "To implement the agreement on the reorganisation of the MUP ..." That is stated on the 2nd of March, so that's after the 23rd of February; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted into evidence, unless it hasn't been admitted already? I think that the actual record was not admitted, but the transcript was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The e-court says it has been admitted as D214, but I note -- is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: MFI, yes, because we do not have the full translation of this document. That's the status, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this a relevant decision for all of you in the MUP, a relevant decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a relevant decision for the entire state, or, rather, then the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all of its institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this also a pretext for you to become involved and to bring the barricade crisis to an end without dramaticising it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Tieger asked me about this, or Ms. Korner - I really cannot recall now - I noted that Serb personnel, of course in agreement with all others in the MUP, played a major role during these 48 hours of the blockade of Sarajevo in order to prevent anything from happening to the population; that is to say, not to have looting, killing, fighting, and so on. It seems to me that I played a major role, myself, together with my co-workers. We kept these barricades under control. We tried to alleviate tensions so that there wouldn't be even more of a rebellion and more destruction of property. In certain parts of town, there were counter-barricades, at Bistrik, Kosevsko Brdo, so a great danger was looming over Sarajevo. It could have been turned into a Beirut, as we had put it then. However, thanks to the member of the police, the Ministry of the Interior, all of this was over without a single incident. Munir Alibabic, of course -- or, rather, the State Security Service of the Sarajevo Centre, turned it in the opposite direction, and they said that Momcilo Mandic, with his co-workers, had organised these barricades and kept them under his control. All of us present here know that if there is a football game, there can be trouble, let alone when thousands and thousands of people go out into the streets and block a city with a population of about 500.000. There are documents attesting to this, that nothing bad happened and that all of this was brought to a peaceful end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I establish that you gave quite a few interviews, and can we say that none of these interviews were made under oath, and none of them were given to you for authentication, and that most of them were distorted by the journalists in the said newspapers, themselves, like the man who broke up the barricades, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. President, as for all of these interviews that were shown to me, these are unknown newspapers or newspapers from the federation, and they kept copying an interview I gave to Serbian Television and then they edited it in different ways, in agreement with the State Security of Sarajevo. I can give answers in all of these respects now. Some of these things never happened that way, but I can answer all those questions now, if you wish to put them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that one of your interviews, which we have not notified the other side about, but we will do so next week, where you speak about the war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter did not understand Mr. Karadzic's question. Could he please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Mandic. The interpreters did not understand your question, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to elicit an answer to this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we bear in mind the fact there were distortions and changes to those interviews, and some were indeed fabricated, in respect of these topics, can we say that your position, which you aired -- which you stated on television, was accurate, whereas all other topics should be dismissed or, rather, reported positions of yours should be dismissed as incorrect? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mean, I appreciate that that may be a question that can be left to the witness, but it seems so abstract and broad, as framed, that it's untethered to any particular documentation, it may not be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we seen this TV interviews or the other interviews? But let us see whether Mr. Mandic can deal with this. Can you answer the question, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not, of course, remember all those interviews. I've seen some of them on Serbian Television and presented some by Mr. Tieger and Ms. Korner. The essence is true, of course, adapted to the current circumstances and the political situation at the time I was granting the interview. As regards all the other interviews and the newspaper articles, I would have to see them to say whether they were distorted, whether they had been produced in security services, or whether field data had been gathered and then articles created on that basis, which is done by these services, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope that next week we will see or read the transcript, but it's still not in e-court and we still have not put the other side on notice. But we will then be able to see what exactly was the position of Mr. Mandic, said to a camera -- in front of a camera in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 -- 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D2020.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an official report and your cover letter to the prime minister -- from the prime minister to the president of the Council for the Constitutional Order and to the minister and the deputy minister of the interior. This is in English. We do not have the Serbian version. I believe that the other side does. This is your cover letter, along with a report concerning developments in Sarajevo between the 1st and 5th of March, 1992, and obviously this pertains to this incident that we are now talking about, the murder of a wedding party member, and barricades and counter-barricades. Do you recall having sent such a report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had to do it in the line of duty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that courtesy of the OTP, we are now getting the Serbian version. Thank you. So could you please look at it, whereas the other participants can use the English version. Can we have the next page, please, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was your cover letter, and this is the report, itself. Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see it after 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report from your department, from your administration at the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the report concerns the event which took place on the 1st of March at 1530, when the parking space in Danila Ilica Street, Nikola Gardovic was killed, and it goes on to say the criminal complaint was filed. I'm reading the English. I'm translating as I go along. That the -- it says "senior," but probably it should be the District Public Prosecutors Office, filed a criminal report against Ramiz Delalic and Suad Sabovic, and then it states their addresses and so on and so forth, and further states that at approximately 2400 hours on the 1st of March, 1992, in Bratstva Jedinstva Street, barricades were erected and that is when the only death occurred, namely, a person was wounded fatally and died -- we can perhaps scroll this up a bit more, please, to see what it says further. Then you say on the 2nd of March, on Mount Trebevic in Stari Grad, another murder was committed, and this is a 100 per cent Muslim settlement, right, a Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you are reporting on all the incidents which had taken place from the 1st to the 5th of March; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the setting up of the barricades and after that, because the barricades stood there for 48 hours and were dismantled on the 2nd of March. But this is until the 5th of March. There are also some other incidents that I reported to the competent state institutions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page? We are not going to read it. I should just like the parties to see it, to see what it is about. The next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, I should just like to read this -- could you scroll it up a bit, please: [In English] "That 20 people received gun-shot wounds. Some were admitted to Kosevo Hospital for treatment, while others were discharged after receiving medical assistance. The following persons sustained bodily injuries." [Interpretation] And here we have a list of the wounded. Can we see the next page, please. So this is the routine-type report, sent to the most important addresses in the republic, because it was a dramatic event and one that had political implications; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We shall just cast a short glance on a document dated the 5th of March, Serbian police from Stari Grad municipality, sent to the ministry and to the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo, one letter. It is 1D1357. We shall not dwell on it at length. We should just like you to corroborate or prove to us the content, the essence of this document. 1D1357, and we have the translation, too. Until we see it, Mr. Minister, can I ask you this: Are those days considered to have been extremely dramatic, in terms of the developments which occurred, which unfolded, and that all the public was apprehensive of what the future held in store.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter by members of the Police Station of Stari Grad of Serbian ethnicity who had worked in that particular station for many years, where they specifically spell out the problems that they have encountered, and they are listed here, let me not read them, which -- and they were common knowledge at the time, at least as far as Stari Grad is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that a pretext for procedures in the Stari Grad, Sokolac, and Pale Public Stations, without any justification? Did they say in these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter did not get the meaning of the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the question again? The interpreters missed that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this event -- this was the culmination of developments and of the disenfranchisement. Was this event -- were these developments a pretext for the procedures of the late Cvijetic and Sokolac and the MUP of Pale; namely, the colleague that had been nominated by the Party of Democratic Action to the police or appointed there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a response to these developments in the centre of Sarajevo, Zoran Cvijetic, who was the chief for the police in Sokolac, which is in an adjacent municipality, dismissed from work all Muslim members on the police force, whereas Malko Koroman would not allow my order to be implemented to the effect that the commander, who had already been elected or nominated of Muslim ethnicity, should be appointed to his post, and at that time there was a conflict, even a physical clash, between me and Malko Koroman.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see 1D1884 in e-court, 1D1884.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until we see that, allow me to describe to you what it is that we will be looking at. This is a letter by the chief of the Public Security Station in Bratunac, Senad Hodzic. As far as I can recall, in Bratunac they had not had a Serb as the commander of the police station, because the chief was a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that they had problems regarding that particular appointment, that of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But Senad Hodzic obviously was politically sensitive enough, because he says: "By the dispatch of the MUP of the 4th of March, a 100 per cent increase in the reserve police force was ordered. "In keeping with that, in a letter to the Bratunac Municipal Secretariat of National Defence, we ask for a list of the necessary free military conscripts according to local communes, respecting the ethnic structure. "After we had received the list and started making the requisite checks, we obtained information that the list included a certain number of Muslim military conscripts who had spent time in Croatia on a part of the training courses within the MUP of Croatia. We do not know on whose orders or recommendation, but it is believed that Serbian citizens do not have enough trust in such future members of the reserve police force." First question: We saw, Mr. Minister, that on the 2nd of March the Presidency adopted all the SDS laws aimed at resolving the crisis, and on the 4th of March it sent an order for the reserve police force to be increased by 100 per cent by taking over unassigned conscripts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please bear with me for a minute. When Their Honours asked me a couple of days ago, I believe, how we learned about those people who came from Croatia, or the illegal manning of the force, one of the ways in which we received such -- obtained such information was this: Namely, chiefs of the police, irrespective of ethnicity, would inform the centre or the headquarters of the Ministry of the Police about these developments, and we knew that people were coming in an inappropriate number and in contravention to the approved staffing scheme and the approved numbers, that they were being armed, they were being given uniforms, and that an army was being created, actually, in the lap, under the wings of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that this was actually two days after the apparently-reached agreement in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this policeman, Hodzic, Senad, is actually acknowledging the fact that Serbian people did not trust enough such potential members of the police reserve force who had been in Croatia, and it is not known at whose orders and at whose recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let us not repeat ourselves. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 65 ter 18271. I don't know if it's an exhibit, a P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The previous one was of the 16th of March, and this letter of yours is dated 18 March, also a telegram. Can you interpret this for us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to all security centres and to the SUP of Sarajevo, to the secretary. It came out of my administration, and it's my dispatch: "On 13 March 1992, by dispatch 10-26, Deputy Minister Dr. Vitomir Zepinic, without the knowledge and approval of this administration, requested information about armaments, munitions, money, and vehicles that had been seized, which were submitted to the MUP for further action. He made this request without authorisation. "I hereby notify you that the deputy minister abused his office of deputy minister, circumventing this administration and putting pressure on certain senior employees of the CSB which I believe to be inappropriate, and it is in contravention of the rules of the service. "At the same time, I hereby notify you that you may not provide any MUP information regarding the Criminal Prevention Services."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we have a translation under --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 1D01 to 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this quite an unusual step by the deputy minister, which indicates that something unusual is happening with weapons, munitions, money, with the police bypassing all normal channels?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter speaks about unlawful conduct on the part of Deputy Minister Zepinic, because it is only the Crime Prevention Service that is in charge of this, and it can be supervised only by the minister or someone authorised in writing by the minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe we have received the translation. It's 1D2018, so that all parties can see the translation as well, and then we can perhaps have this document admitted. Could we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the 65 ter number of this is 1D1218, and it has been marked for identification as Exhibit D197. But having heard the author's confirmation now, I think we can admit this document, unless it is objected to. Yes, it will be admitted now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall that the Defence has used this document before, but never mind. In any case, it's been admitted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court says that you used this document with Mr. van Lynden on 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the confusion was that the first document called up for translation was not related to this particular B/C/S document. The document we have on screen now is -- I don't know what the confusion was in the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, this is a totally different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies. This is a totally different document. We need to admit it separately. So the document we are dealing with is 65 ter 18271. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly look at 65 ter 1492. 1492. There is an English version as well. Can we see page 2, and English page 2. Under D, we see "Constituent Units," and under number 2, towards the bottom: [In English] "Police trade and other constituents units may establish and maintain relations and links with the other republics," and so on. [Interpretation] This is a fundamental principle for the future structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed here, and we see that constituent units have the right to their own police force. Can we see the next page. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to number 4, towards the top: "Members of the nations who would be in a minority in a particular constituent unit would receive protection similar to that in Article 2(3) of the draft convention." Does this mean, Minister, that it was envisaged that every constituent unit have minorities as well, and that there was no transfer or exchange of population planned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document is an exhibit. There's no need to go further into it, but let me ask you this: In my understanding, the entire indictment against me hangs upon a thread, and that thread is the allegation that we intended to get rid of Muslims and Croats from territories that Bosnian Serbs laid rights upon, and these rights were not so questionable. Even the European Union accepted them. But when we speak about the separation of Muslims and Croats, is it really the case that that implies throwing them out of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never been aware of any such views before the war. These are the views of European mediators, diplomats, who were negotiating with leaders of ruling national parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina was Yugoslavia, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall -- and we'll probably deal with this next week, but let me just remind you. On the 12th of May, you were sworn in as a minister in Banja Luka, minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as the minister of justice of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, did you attend a ceremony in the Police Academy of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next week, we will deal with it in greater detail, but I'm glad you confirmed you attended that ceremony. We will show it later. This has been admitted into evidence already. Can I now ask for 65 ter 01016. Minister, this is also your document, in which you referred to the document that was passed on the 23rd of February and 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I just rise for a housekeeping matter. The accused referred to the fact that the previous document had been admitted, but there was no reference to the exhibit number, which might be helpful in the transcript, which I believe is P782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document being referred to by the accused is Exhibit P1116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, this is a rather well-known dispatch in which you notify about the decisions of the Assembly of the Serbian People. And in line two, it says -- I'll read the first sentence: "At its meeting held on 27 March 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in accordance with the political orientation of the Serbian people and the Sarajevo Agreement, promulgated the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This reference to the Sarajevo Agreement, is it a reference to the agreements with the European Union, led by Cutileiro and Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mediators were Jose Cutileiro, a Portuguese diplomat, and Lord Carrington, a UK diplomat. And what we were looking at before were the basic principles to be developed later, and they were known as the Lisbon Agreement and the Sarajevo Agreement, the fundamental principles of the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this dispatch, among other things, was in keeping with those agreements that had been reached with the help of European mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact page, but will you probably remember, in the trial of Mr. Krajisnik, the Prosecution asked you whether you were aware that you had started a civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina by this telegram, and you answered that you were acting in keeping with the decisions of the Assembly and the Council for National Defence. Let me ask you, was the Council for National Defence established as an advisory body of the Assembly of the Serbian People on the 27th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that is not in dispute. We have it in transcripts. But what was said at the Presidency about the crisis in Kupres, and you mentioned a multi-ethnic delegation going to Kupres and Zivinice, et cetera, do you remember that Croatian paramilitaries entered Bosanski Brod on the 3rd of March and perpetrated crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember events in Bosanski Brod, but I also remember Kupres, because I believe I went there with one of my colleagues. We went out into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I suppose this document is in evidence. We've heard the number. And towards the bottom, it says: "The contents of this dispatch needs to be notified to all employees of the MUP of the SR BH for the purposes of subjective and timely information and to avoid possible incidents and other undesirable consequences." Does that include Croats and Muslims working in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is self-explanatory. Everything is well explained. What the legal basis is, the organisation involved, et cetera, it is mentioned expressly. And there is also a supplement to this dispatch, sent the following day, in consultation with my other colleagues from the joint MUP, where we sent a dispatch to inform that pending the resolution of the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least as far as the police is concerned, we will have joint training and education, joint disposal of all materiel and equipment, and all services related to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have that document. Let me just remind you about one other thing. Do you recall that on 25 March a paramilitary unit from Croatia made an incursion and killed a father and son at a petrol station at Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 26th of March, that same crowd, unchecked by anyone, went on to the nearby village of Sijekovac and killed everything and everyone there, including the livestock?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one in a series of events that were gaining momentum in the war-affected areas, because neighbouring Croatia was at war, and the war was spilling over with ever greater force across the Una and Drina River into Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is just one example, and there are more of them. Such incidents were becoming more and more frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this crowd was not stopped by anyone; not by the police, because they didn't have enough men, allegedly, nor the army, nor the paramilitary units, because they didn't exist at the time, and they were able to go on unchecked as far as they pleased?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was wallowing in these problems that we are discussing now, and an armed, irregular unit from Croatia came in and perpetrated a massacre in Sijekovac. They killed a father and son at the petrol station and then went back -- came back after that incident. Bosnia and Herzegovina was undefended. It was part of Yugoslavia, but defended by no one. Croats and Muslims did not want an army. Serbs wanted to stay in Yugoslavia. Everyone want to do go their own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript says that Croats and Muslims did not want an army, but the truth is they did not trust the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they didn't trust the army, and there was no one to defend the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was still at that time part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a document, minutes of the Assembly session of the 27 March, when we established this National Defence Council. Do you recall that Muslims formed the National Defence Council, at least, on the 10th or 11th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We've been through this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll have a break, Mr. Karadzic, for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I briefly ask for a document in e-court, 1D2022. Could the Serbian version please be given to the witness. And in e-court, we're going to see the translation. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I inform you, Minister, that this is another one of your documents. The date is the 26th of March, 1992, that is to say, the day when a massacre occurred in Sijekovac. You are trying -- actually, a multi-ethnic delegation is going to Kupres in order to defuse the crisis in the relationship between the Serbs and Croats, as is stated here, in your municipality. Do you remember the document? Do you remember going there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your signature. Can you just tell us whether you managed to have the tensions eased during this meeting and avoid a conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, already on the 3rd of April, there was a major clash there between paramilitary formations of the Croats, on the one hand, and, on the other side, the Yugoslav People's Army; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was addressed to who, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sent to the chief of police in the place that we were supposed to go to. A delegation had been announced from the police headquarters, and the actual names of the members of the delegation were listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was asking to what SJB it was addressed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Public Security Station, Kupres; that is, to the chief of police in the town that we were supposed to go to. So it's basically the local police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D1889, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your telegram, dated the 1st of April, 1992, and it represents continuity, in view of the previous telegram. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a joint dispatch of members of the collegium of the minister of police of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As we can see here from the first sentence, it is based on the Sarajevo Agreement on the possible future organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone attended, all assistant ministers and the deputy, except for Minister Delimustafic, himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic was present as well; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "everybody," I mean all of those who were in the professional collegium of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to recommend the entire document to the participants in these proceedings. These are agreements that are being reached at political level among the three ethnic communities and under the chairmanship of the European Community, or, rather, with the mediation of Carrington and Cutileiro; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this was an agreement among all the participants in this meeting. I remember very well that we greeted each other and that Brano Kvesic and Bruno Stojic went to Herzegovina as representatives of the Croat people in the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They went to work on the basis of this agreement; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this document envisage what it is that remains shared at the level of the republic, as far as police work is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the second page in B/C/S, but I do know that we agreed that education, material and financial operations, joint services, should remain shared until the political status of Bosnia-Herzegovina is fully resolved; that is to say, until the principles that we discussed a moment ago are adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask for the lower part of the Serbian page and probably page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I forgot to mention that it was agreed that education, schooling, should be shared or joint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So legislation, policy, education, and other things, whereas the executive will belong to the constituent units, as envisaged in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the Cutileiro Agreement, President, that is to say, the Sarajevo and Lisbon Agreement, that was the basis upon which this law was passed, and I sent this dispatch on the basis of that. All of us agreed here that we should work on the basis of these standards until the way in which the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are to be established is finally agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we scroll up in Serbian so that we see who it was that signed this and on behalf of who this was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this mean it was the collegium of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and all the persons who attended the meeting are listed here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for 10835, please. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram that is basically simultaneous. Actually, the 31st of March is the date on this document, whereas your document is the 1st of April, but they do have some kind of correlation. It was signed by the minister of the interior, who is disassociating himself in this telegram from the agreement that all of you had reached at that collegium meeting referred to in the previous document. Do you recall this document.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, he is disassociating himself from the dispatch that you sent on the 31st of March, not from this that occurred on the 1st of April; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I remind you that our constant objection was during the negotiations that the Muslim side is operating along a double track, that Izetbegovic is saying one thing to me and that Silajdzic is saying something different in Europe and in Brussels, does that seem to you as part of this double-track operation under pressure exerted by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister had to write this under the pressure exerted on him by his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mr. Delimustafic a witness in the proceedings against you, where you were acquitted? You were charged with having committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, unless the OTP had already tendered it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not already admitted, by its number, D390? It's your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What's the number of that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 10835. The current document has been admitted as Exhibit P1117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, a P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D1908. We are going to focus on part of the testimony of Mr. Delimustafic's testimony under oath in Bosnia. I actually missed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you acquitted of having committed war crimes before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, on the basis of this, there seem to be some foreign judges, and I believe that that is why you were acquitted. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two people from this court, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. This was just an observation I made in passing. It can be struck from the record. It actually reflects our domestic situation. We are not happy with the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Page 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: An unnecessary comment, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I withdrew the comment. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 7. In response to the question put by Defence counsel -- page 6 in English, actually. Serbian, 7, and it's page 6 in English. That's it. Counsel Serdarevic, he's a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He is asking Mr. Delimustafic: "During the night between the 1st and 2nd of March, in relation to the barricades, after the killing of a wedding party member at Bascarsija, could you tell us what the minister of the interior did to resolve the barricades issue?" And Mr. Delimustafic says: "Well, our duty was to unblock the city, and as Momo was the assistant minister, the collegium concluded that he should go there and try to have the barricades removed." Counsel: "Do you want to say -- could you say who erected the barricades?" And Delimustafic says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the proper page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the second half of the page -- [In English] Could answer, Serdarevic, Counsel Serdarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then Serdarevic says: "Do you want to say -- could you say who erected the barricades?" And Mr. Delimustafic says: "Well, the people dissatisfied with the killing of the wedding party member." Is this confirmation of the reasons why the barricades were erected, and did it come from the top level of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is the killing of the wedding party member that caused the erection of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, Mr. President, I believe that that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was wondering where this process of referring to witness testimony in Mr. Mandic's case was going, but it appears to be an attempt to corroborate the witness's testimony with the testimony of witnesses in the previous case. We've had previous discussions about the meaning of statements and the use of -- the difference between contemporaneous documentation or statements produced for purposes of legal proceedings generally, statements produced for purposes of these particular legal proceedings, and maybe in between those, statements produced for legal proceedings very closely related to these proceedings. I raise that to seek some guidance on that, because it's clear that both parties may find themselves interested in various aspects of testimony related to cases undertaken by Bosnian authorities on related or overlapping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I'm following you. You are objecting to putting these questions to the witness by the accused, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't precluding all aspects or all conceivable references to such testimony, although I couldn't think of one off-hand that might fall properly within the guide-lines, as I understood them. But now it seems to be that we're trying to -- that there's an effort made to take testimony given in previous cases and introduce it into this case, and I would have thought that given the nature of the guide-lines, given the nature of the 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater process, that that sort of importation for that sort of purpose is not what the Court envisioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it seems to me the problem is this: that it's a reference to a case which has been the subject of a final determination, but it is impossible, by the very nature of such litigation, to determine which evidence was accepted and which evidence wasn't. Ergo, we would simply going down the road of satellite litigation, where it could not be proved, one way or another, whether the matters that have been referred to have been accepted or not accepted, and this Court would not be in a position to accept or not to accept that testimony. The fact that it's repeated in this Tribunal theoretically brings it into the ambit of the determination, but I think you're right; if one party goes down that road, then both parties are entitled to go down that road, and I repeat what I said a few days ago. The effect would be satellite litigation, which would add weeks, if not months, to the proceedings. That's an observation rather than a ruling, but I know that Dr. Karadzic has heard what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can get further clarification, Mr. Tieger. You referred to our guide-lines. Is it not related to the admission of documents or evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in that connection, what I had in mind at that particular moment was the fact that we have had some difficulty with the issues surrounding the admissibility and the timing of the admissibility of documents -- of official documents contemporaneously produced by, for example, the Bosnian Serb political and military authorities. Now, that -- and as a general matter, we've distinguished that from witness testimony which has been subject to the guide-lines provided within the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal and have been treated quite separately. And I say that because the admissibility and weight factors surrounding contemporaneous documents produced at the time not for litigation, I think, is clearly -- clearly presents more direct, simpler issues, and there's no dispute, I think, about the broad admissibility of those factors. And, in fact, the parties have been consistently or largely united in their views that those documents are admitted. So I use this as a point of contrast to something like this, where we're now on the verge of re-litigating or contemplating the re-litigation of entirely separate cases, and I think the Rules envision that, for the most part, parties can call witnesses, rather than attempt to import litigation -- extracts of litigation in previous proceedings where those contemplated witnesses have provided testimony. Otherwise, we -- in many instances, there wouldn't have been no need for the elaboration preparation of 92 ter packages and the presence of those witnesses here in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Mr. Tieger, you could rise when Mr. Karadzic was about to tender this transcript as evidence, but he was putting the question to the witness, who was there, hearing that evidence, Mr. Delimustafic's evidence. So speaking for myself, I see no problem putting that question at this moment. Mr. Karadzic, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. With all due respect to the other side, my distinguished colleague, I should like to thank the OTP because they disclosed this document according to Rule 68 in Batch 214 and recommended to the Defence to use it. On the other hand, Prosecution witnesses here have contended that the barricades were erected as our response to the referendum, although this was an all-Bosnia referendum, and this was not the case. There were no barricades elsewhere; only in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's proper to discuss in detail in the presence of the witness. We'll confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber wanted to deliberate on this matter further, so I would advise you to skip to another matter, leaving this matter -- deferring this matter to next week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing against that; namely, if what is relevant is in the transcript, for this not to be admitted. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So move on to another topic or another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just conclude, Mr. Minister. This is confirmation that Mr. Delimustafic contested, under pressure -- all right, all right, very well. Can we now see 65 ter 05422. We'll go over this one very briefly just to see the further implementation in the police of this. This is the Centre of Security Services in Banja Luka.
